Pollack (Pollachius pollachius) exhibit a maximum recorded body length of 130 centimeters [Li = 130 centimeters], a size that positions them among the larger gadoids in the northeastern Atlantic. Sexual maturation, marked by the initial activation of the gonads, is typically observed once individuals attain a total length of 41 centimeters [Lp = 41 centimeters], a relatively early onset of puberty for a species of this ultimate size. Field studies indicate that females at this length correspond to a wet weight of approximately 657 grams [Wwp = approximately 657 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions routinely applied to this taxon. The length at which 50 percent of the population is mature aligns closely with these measurements, suggesting a consistent pattern of reproductive development across most of the species’ geographic range. In contrast, the largest reproductively active females can reach an ultimate wet weight of 18100 grams [Wwi = 18100 grams], underscoring the considerable scope for somatic growth that continues well after the onset of breeding. This substantial size disparity between maturing and fully grown individuals reflects a life-history strategy in which moderate early reproduction does not preclude extensive late-life somatic investment, a pattern characteristic of many iteroparous marine fishes.

At a prevailing water temperature of 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C], the mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) was recorded at 7% [GSI = 7%]. The index was calculated from dissected ovaries and eviscerated body mass, following standard ichthyological protocols.

The early life stages of Pollack are initiated by the emergence of yolk-sac larvae following a brief incubation period. The age at which larvae begin first exogenous feeding for eggs incubated at 9.4 °C [T = 9.4 °C] is approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days]. This rapid developmental rate is characteristic of gadoid embryos reared at moderate thermal regimes, where elevated temperatures accelerate cleavage and organogenesis. The wet weight of a newly emerged larva is extremely small, estimated at 0.0008 grams [Wwb = 0.0008 grams], a mass derived from the average egg diameter of 1.15 millimeters recorded for the congeneric species Pollachius virens. This minute starting size means that larvae are highly dependent on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatch before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. The transition from lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva to first exogenous feeding represents a critical bottleneck in the species’ early life history, with survival contingent upon the timely availability of suitable planktonic prey.

Longevity records for Pollack suggest that individuals can attain a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of the northeastern Atlantic, where mean annual water temperatures approximate 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C]. This lifespan is moderate among gadoids, falling between the shorter-lived Atlantic cod and the longer-lived tusk. The species exhibits a gradual senescence pattern, with annual mortality rates increasing only after the tenth year of life. Growth continues throughout most of the lifespan, albeit at a decelerating rate, such that the asymptotic length of 130 centimeters is approached but rarely exceeded. The combination of a 15-year lifespan and delayed senescence allows females multiple reproductive seasons over their lifetime, contributing to population stability through repeated spawning events. Tag-recapture studies indicate that the oldest recorded individuals frequently correspond to the largest females, which also display the highest fecundity per spawning event, highlighting the demographic importance of older age classes.

Regarding the timing of first reproduction, Pollack typically spawn for the first time at an age of approximately 4 years in the wild. Post-hatching, the free-swimming larva enters a pelagic phase that lasts several months before metamorphosis and subsequent settlement into demersal juvenile habitat. The length at which puberty is attained, 41 centimeters [Lp = 41 centimeters], is similar to that observed in related species and corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 657 grams [Wwp = approximately 657 grams], a mass that is reached after roughly two to three years of rapid juvenile growth. The species thereby exhibits a relatively fast juvenile growth rate that allows individuals to transition into the reproductively mature fraction of the population well before the completion of somatic growth. This life-history schedule, combining early maturation with continued late-life growth, reinforces the iteroparous strategy evident across much of the genus Pollachius.
